extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction and prose writers (general creative-writing audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for prose writers on vocabulary, grammar, sentence and paragraph-level choices, and dialogue; emphasizes clarity, voice, and reader-first decisions. Focused on the stylistic tools a fiction/prose writer should keep 'on top of the toolbox.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary — use the first appropriate word
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic rule of vocabulary is use the first word that comes to your mind, if it is appropriate and colorful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dress up vocabulary looking for long words out of shame for short ones; don’t use obscure or pretentious words when a simple one will do (e.g., don’t use “emolument” when you mean “tip”). Improve vocabulary mostly by reading rather than by conscious word-hoarding. Consider audience and appropriateness (you may choose cruder or plainer words if the audience deems them acceptable — e.g., use “take a shit” if the voice/audience allows, otherwise choose a suitable euphemism). Examples and anti-patterns: avoid deliberate inflation of diction (pet-peeve phrases like “that’s so cool,” “at this point in time”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar — know the rudiments and keep them available
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a rudimentary grasp of grammar (parts of speech, sentence construction) so you can be 'certain of doing well' and know when rule-breaking is deliberate and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grammar is a tool to keep your thoughts on their feet: nouns and verbs are indispensable. If you don't grasp the rudiments you cannot reliably judge your own writing. Use basic references (Warriner’s, Strunk & White) to refresh ‘rusty’ skills. Follow rules unless you are certain your deliberate exception improves the writing. Example rule cited: form possessives with ’s even when the word ends in s (Thomas’s bike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active verbs; avoid the passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor active constructions where the subject performs the action rather than having action done to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive is often weak, circuitous, and tortuous; use active voice to energize prose (e.g., “The meeting’s at seven” vs. passive alternatives). Exceptions exist: passive may be acceptable when logically the inanimate or irrelevantly acted-upon thing is best as subject (but still prefer active if possible). The author’s examples show how active voice clarifies and strengthens writing and how passive often signals timidity or false authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adverbs (especially in dialogue attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs are often a crutch of timid writers and have a tendency to proliferate into weak prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: root out adverbs—'the road to hell is paved with adverbs.' In dialogue attribution, use adverbs only in the rarest occasions; prefer simple verbs (said) over constructions like 'she shouted menacingly' or 'he pleaded abjectly.' Overuse creates clichés and comical 'Swifties.' If the preceding context makes the manner clear, the adverb is redundant. Exception: when necessary for clarity and no better verb/context exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue attribution — use 'said' and avoid showy attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form of dialogue attribution is said/he said/she said; avoid colorful verb-attributions and adverbial modifiers to describe how someone spoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t replace simple attribution with inflated verbs (grated, jerked out) or adverb-laden lines. Such choices often read as pulpy or amateurish. If you need to convey manner, prefer context, action beats, or stronger verbs that actually add information, but default to 'said.' Larry McMurtry is recommended as a model for sparing attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and render dialect/colloquial speech appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-standard, phonetically rendered, or street vocabulary is valid vocabulary when handled skillfully and suitable for the work’s voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers like Tom Wolfe and Elmore Leonard can translate street speech to the page effectively; phonetic renderings (e.g., 'Egggh, whaddaya?') can be powerful if authentic. Be judicious: such material may enter the dictionary eventually, but it should fit character and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence simplicity as a safety net — use noun+verb clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple noun-verb sentences provide a reliable path when complex structures threaten coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take comfort in basic sentences (Rocks explode; Jane transmits). Strunk & White caution against too many simple sentences in a row, but they serve as a safety net when you're lost in complex clauses. Use simple sentences to vary rhythm; avoid an entire piece made solely of fragments, but accept fragments where they serve voice and pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fragments and single-sentence paragraphs strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-sentence paragraphs and fragments can vary pace, streamline narration, and resemble speech — but can be overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fiction, brief paragraphs and fragments are legitimate 'beats' that can create tension and freshness (examples from Kellerman). In expository prose, stick to fuller, topic-sentence-and-support paragraphs. Avoid overuse of fragments which can stiffen or embarrass if misapplied; rewrite later if necessary during revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphs are the basic unit of writing — organize by beat or topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph form (visual blocks/white space) signals ease/hardness of reading and organizes coherence; in expository prose use topic sentence + amplification, in fiction let paragraphs follow the beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at page layout: lots of short paragraphs and white space make a book feel 'easy'; dense paragraphs feel packed and idea-heavy. For expository writing, craft a clear topic sentence followed by explanatory/supporting sentences. In fiction, let paragraph breaks follow rhythm, dialogue shifts, or transitions; paragraph choices can mark character, setting, or stage direction. Paragraphs can range from one word to many pages — learn the 'beat' through lots of practice and reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reader the primary concern — clarity over affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Always write to make the reader welcome; avoid affectation, showing-off, or fearful attempts to seem authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad writing often stems from fear and timid affectation. Choices (vocabulary, voice, grammar) should serve the reader’s understanding and pleasure. Avoid defining writing as 'good' or 'bad' out of affectation; instead focus on clear choices that help the reader forget they’re reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to break rules — but only if you can do it well
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule-breaking in rhetoric can be effective, but only when the writer is certain of doing well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strunk’s caveat: 'Unless he is certain of doing well, [the writer] will probably do best to follow the rules.' If you lack a rudimentary grasp of grammar and form, experimental violations will likely harm clarity. Practice and reading build the judgment to break rules intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and pretentious phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Purge overused and pretentious phrases that add nothing to clarity or voice (author lists personal dislikes as examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples to avoid: 'the fact that,' 'along these lines,' 'at this point in time,' 'at the end of the day,' and social clichés like 'That's so cool.' Such phrases often signal weak thinking or lazy phrasing; remove them during revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve tools by reading rather than forced drills
rubrics_metrics.description: You will improve vocabulary and stylistic sense chiefly by reading; don’t obsess on artificial vocabulary-building exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put vocabulary on the top shelf of your toolbox and don't make conscious, showy efforts to improve it — reading will supply the growth. Similarly, refresh grammar by consulting compact references as needed rather than trying to relearn everything from scratch.
